explanations.explanation: That's their question, word for word: "Tell us, how did this wicked thing happen?" (Judges 20:3) I think they want the account from someone who was there. And that's who steps up next, the Levite, the husband of the murdered woman.

explanations.answer: Who will be king over them
explanations.explanation: Nobody at Mizpah asks about a king. Their question is about the wicked thing that happened. The book does say, "In those days Israel had no king…" (Judges 21:25), but that's the writer talking, not the crowd asking.
The numbers in this passage are real, but this isn't the question. The Israelites ask how this wicked thing happened. Counting the Benjamites comes later, when they show up ready to fight.

He says the men of Gibeah rose up against him in the night, surrounded the house and intended to kill him. Then he says they abused his concubine and she died. This is a heavy part of the story, friend, and I think it hurts to read.

The Levite does say it. He tells the assembly the men of Gibeah "intended to kill me" (Judges 20:5). Then he adds that they abused his concubine and she died. I'll say it plainly: this is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Gibeah's men did a disgraceful act in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the reason he gives. He says he sent her throughout the land "because they had committed a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel." (Judges 20:6) He points the whole nation at what Gibeah's men did.

explanations.answer: He wanted the tribes to choose a king
explanations.explanation: A king never comes up in his speech. The Levite names one reason, and it's the lewd and disgraceful act the men of Gibeah committed in Israel (Judges 20:6). The whole assembly hears it from him.

explanations.answer: He wanted Benjamin to pay him back
explanations.explanation: He says nothing here about being paid back. His reason is the act itself, the lewd and disgraceful thing done in Israel (Judges 20:6). Then he hands the matter to the assembly for their advice and verdict.

explanations.answer: Not one of them will go home
explanations.explanation: They say it together: "Not one of us will return to his tent or to his house." (Judges 20:8) That's a whole nation putting its life on hold. Nobody is slipping out the back.

explanations.answer: Each of them will go home to pray
explanations.explanation: Going home is exactly what they say they won't do. The people say, "Not one of us will return to his tent or to his house." (Judges 20:8) Prayer does come up later, but not as a trip home.

explanations.answer: Only the leaders will stay behind
explanations.explanation: It isn't just the leaders. The text says all the people stood as one man when they said it (Judges 20:8). So when the Israelites say "Not one of us," the whole crowd means every single one.

Provisions, the supplies an army needs while it marches. They take ten men out of every hundred, a hundred out of every thousand and a thousand out of every ten thousand to supply them (Judges 20:10). No bakery runs on good intentions, friend. You need supplies, and so does an army.
Horses aren't mentioned in this plan. The text says these men are taken "to supply provisions for the army" (Judges 20:10). Supplies are what keep an army fed and moving.
No chariots here. The men from every tribe are chosen to supply provisions for the army when it goes to Gibeah (Judges 20:10). The plan is about keeping the army supplied.

Death is the word. They ask Benjamin to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah "so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil." (Judges 20:13) It's a serious demand, and it comes before any fighting starts.
Shame isn't the word. Israel's message says the wicked men are to be put to death, so Israel can be purged of this evil (Judges 20:13). The message is serious and direct.
The message doesn't talk about flight. It says to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah "so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil." (Judges 20:13) That's the word they chose.
The text says the opposite. "But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites." (Judges 20:13) They don't hand anyone over. Instead they gather at Gibeah to fight.
The text says it right there: "But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites." (Judges 20:13) Nobody gets handed over. Benjamin comes out of its cities to fight instead.

explanations.answer: Sling a stone at a hair without missing
explanations.explanation: Each of those 700 left-handers "could sling a stone at a hair without missing." (Judges 20:16) A hair, friend. I once stamped the same cookie twice, a hair's width off, and called it a design. These men were not doing that.

explanations.answer: Shoot an arrow through a ring
explanations.explanation: No arrows or rings here. The text says each of the 700 select left-handers could sling a stone at a hair without missing (Judges 20:16). Slingers, not archers.

explanations.answer: Throw a spear across a river
explanations.explanation: The text has no spears and no river. These 700 select left-handers are slingers, and each could sling a stone at a hair without missing (Judges 20:16). That's the skill the text names.
That's how the text describes them: 400,000 swordsmen, "each one an experienced warrior." (Judges 20:17) These are not beginners. Keep that in mind, because the numbers look very lopsided on paper.

explanations.answer: Mostly young men new to battle
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. These 400,000 swordsmen are each one an experienced warrior (Judges 20:17). Nobody in that army is new to this.
The text doesn't describe them that way. It says these swordsmen were each one an experienced warrior (Judges 20:17). They came ready, with swords already in hand.
It doesn't happen that way. The Benjamites come out of Gibeah and cut down 22,000 Israelites on the battlefield that day (Judges 20:21). The huge army does not win easily.
Right, it goes the other way. The Benjamites come out of Gibeah and cut down 22,000 Israelites that day (Judges 20:21). All those experienced warriors, and the first day still goes to Benjamin.

explanations.answer: Weeping and asking Him what to do
explanations.explanation: That's what they do. They "wept before the LORD until evening, inquiring of Him" about whether to draw near for battle again (Judges 20:23). After losing 22,000 men, they bring their question to Him.

explanations.answer: Building an altar out of stones
explanations.explanation: No altar of stones here. The text says they went up and wept before the LORD until evening, inquiring of Him (Judges 20:23). They bring their question and their tears.

explanations.answer: Reading the Law out loud together
explanations.explanation: Nothing is read aloud in this scene. They wept before the LORD until evening and inquired of Him (Judges 20:23). Weeping and asking is what the text tells us they do.

That's His answer: "Go up against them." (Judges 20:23) That follows their question about drawing near for battle against their brothers the Benjamites. Hard to hear after a day like that, and I think it was.
He does tell them to go. The LORD answered, "Go up against them." (Judges 20:23) That's His reply to their question about fighting their brothers the Benjamites again.
Benjamin "cut down another 18,000 Israelites, all of them armed with swords." (Judges 20:25) Add that to the first day's 22,000 and it's a heavy loss. This is the hardest stretch of the story.

explanations.answer: Benjamin runs back inside the walls
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The Benjamites come out of Gibeah against Israel and cut down another 18,000 Israelites (Judges 20:25). Israel takes a second heavy loss.

explanations.answer: Both armies pull back before noon
explanations.explanation: Neither army pulls back in the text. The Benjamites come out of Gibeah and cut down another 18,000 Israelites that same day (Judges 20:25). It's another hard day for Israel.
That day they "fasted until evening and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD." (Judges 20:26) They sat weeping, fasted and brought offerings. All of it is before Him.
No idols come down in this scene. The Israelites sit weeping before the LORD, fast until evening and present burnt offerings and peace offerings (Judges 20:26). That's what the text gives us.
The text doesn't mention a new leader. They go up to Bethel, weep, fast until evening and present burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD (Judges 20:26). Then they inquire of Him.

They ask: "Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?" (Judges 20:28) That's a new part of the question. After two days like that, I think stopping was on the table.
They do add it. They ask, "Should we again go out to battle against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop?" (Judges 20:28) The question now includes stopping, and the LORD answers it.

explanations.answer: He'll deliver Benjamin into their hand tomorrow
explanations.explanation: The LORD answers, "Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand." (Judges 20:28) Two hard days, then a promise with a day attached. Tomorrow is the day.

explanations.answer: Judah will win the battle alone tomorrow
explanations.explanation: That isn't the promise. Judah was named to go first back in the first inquiry (Judges 20:18). This time the LORD says, "Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand." (Judges 20:28)

explanations.answer: Benjamin will give up within seven days
explanations.explanation: No seven days here. The LORD says, "Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand." (Judges 20:28) The promise is for tomorrow.
The Benjamites came out against them and "began to attack the people as before." (Judges 20:31) They were drawn away from the city as they did it. It looks like the same story as days one and two.
The text has Benjamin starting it. The Benjamites come out against them, are drawn away from the city and begin to attack the people as before (Judges 20:31). Israel's plan comes after that.

explanations.answer: Both armies wait all day long
explanations.explanation: Nobody waits all day. The Benjamites come out and begin to attack as before, killing about thirty men of Israel in the fields and on the roads (Judges 20:31). The fighting starts right away.

That's the plan. The Israelites say, "Let us retreat and draw them away from the city onto the roads." (Judges 20:32) Meanwhile the Benjamites are saying they're winning as before. Israel's retreat is part of the plan.
They do plan it. The Israelites say, "Let us retreat and draw them away from the city onto the roads." (Judges 20:32) Benjamin thinks it's the same as before, and the retreat is part of the plan.
The text says they can't. "The Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them." (Judges 20:34) They're in a fierce battle and have no idea what's coming.
The text says it plainly: "But the Benjamites did not realize that disaster was upon them." (Judges 20:34) The battle is fierce, and they still can't see it coming. They only realize later.

The text says, "The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel." (Judges 20:35) Israel had an ambush and big numbers, and the text still names Him. It matches the promise from the day before (Judges 20:28).
Judah went first at the start (Judges 20:18), but the text names someone else here. "The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel." (Judges 20:35) He's the one it credits.

Phinehas, who served before the ark, is mentioned earlier (Judges 20:28), but he isn't named here. The text says, "The LORD defeated Benjamin in the presence of Israel." (Judges 20:35) He's the one it credits.
They look behind them and see "the whole city going up in smoke." (Judges 20:40) That column of smoke was the signal Israel had set up (Judges 20:38). Everything changes in that moment.
The ambush isn't leaving. When the column of smoke goes up, the Benjamites look behind them and see the whole city going up in smoke (Judges 20:40). The ambush had already done its work.

explanations.answer: Their own men coming to help
explanations.explanation: No help is coming in this scene. The Benjamites look behind them and see the whole city going up in smoke (Judges 20:40). That's the sight that stops them.

That's what the text says. The men of Israel turned back on them, and "the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them." (Judges 20:41) A minute earlier they thought they were winning.
They are. The men of Israel turn back on them, and "the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them." (Judges 20:41) Then they run.
They don't outrun it. They fled toward the wilderness, "but the battle overtook them." (Judges 20:42) Running doesn't get them away.

The text says they fled toward the wilderness, "but the battle overtook them." (Judges 20:42) They can't get away from it. Israel surrounds and pursues them, and overtakes them easily near Gibeah (Judges 20:43).
That's where the 600 go: "to the rock of Rimmon." (Judges 20:47) They fled into the wilderness and stayed there. Only 600 men are left from all those Benjamite swordsmen.
That place isn't in this story. The 600 turn and flee into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20:47). That's the place the text names.
The text sends them somewhere else. The 600 flee into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20:47). That's where they stay.
They stayed there four months (Judges 20:47). That's a long stretch of hiding. The text only says they stayed, and I won't guess what those months were like.
It's longer than days. The text says the 600 men stayed at the rock of Rimmon four months (Judges 20:47). Months, not days.
Months, not years. The text says four months at the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20:47). I spent years in the back of a junk drawer once, so believe me, I'd notice the difference.

That's what the text says. The men of Israel "burned down all the cities in their path." (Judges 20:48) Along with that, they put the cities to the sword, including the animals and everything else they found. This is a heavy ending to the passage.
The text doesn't hand the cities to anyone. The men of Israel put the cities to the sword and burned down all the cities in their path (Judges 20:48). It's a heavy ending.
They don't stay standing. The text says the men of Israel "burned down all the cities in their path." (Judges 20:48) It's a hard thing to read, and the text doesn't soften it.
